dimensions.label: Taxes & government spending
dimensions.minus: Raise taxes, especially on high earners and corporations, to fund expanded public programs
dimensions.plus: Keep taxes low and limit government spending and new programs

dimensions.label: Housing growth & land use
dimensions.minus: Preserve local control and neighborhood character; limit density and large new developments
dimensions.plus: Build much more housing: allow more density, reduce zoning limits, speed up permits

dimensions.label: Renters & landlords
dimensions.minus: Stronger renter protections: rent control, eviction limits, tenant legal aid
dimensions.plus: More flexibility for property owners: fewer rent and eviction rules

dimensions.label: Policing & criminal justice
dimensions.minus: Shift resources to prevention and alternatives; reduce incarceration and sentence lengths
dimensions.plus: Expand police staffing and enforcement; tougher penalties for crime

dimensions.label: Homelessness response
dimensions.minus: Housing-first: provide housing and services without preconditions; avoid enforcement-led approaches
dimensions.plus: Enforcement-led: clear encampments, enforce camping bans, require treatment or shelter acceptance

dimensions.label: Climate & energy
dimensions.minus: Aggressive climate action: faster emissions cuts, stricter environmental rules, phase out fossil fuels
dimensions.plus: Prioritize energy affordability and reliability; fewer environmental mandates, keep oil and gas production

dimensions.label: Workers & business
dimensions.minus: Stronger worker protections: higher minimum wages, union power, mandated benefits
dimensions.plus: Business flexibility: fewer labor mandates and regulations, lower costs for employers

dimensions.label: Immigration
dimensions.minus: Protect immigrants: sanctuary policies, limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement
dimensions.plus: Cooperate with federal immigration enforcement; stricter immigration policy

dimensions.label: Education
dimensions.minus: Invest in traditional public schools; limit charter expansion; support teachers' unions
dimensions.plus: Expand school choice and charters; greater parental control over curriculum

dimensions.label: Abortion & LGBTQ+ rights
dimensions.minus: Protect and expand abortion access and LGBTQ+ legal protections
dimensions.plus: More restrictions on abortion; emphasis on traditional or religious values

dimensions.label: Guns
dimensions.minus: Stricter gun laws: more restrictions on purchase, carry, and types of firearms
dimensions.plus: Protect gun rights: fewer restrictions on ownership and carry

dimensions.label: Health care
dimensions.minus: Government-run or publicly expanded coverage (e.g. single-payer, expanded Medi-Cal)
dimensions.plus: Market-based health care with private insurance and less government role

dimensions.label: Transportation
dimensions.minus: Prioritize transit, bike, and pedestrian infrastructure, even at the cost of car lanes and parking
dimensions.plus: Prioritize roads, driving, and parking; skeptical of reallocating street space

dimensions.label: Elections & voting
dimensions.minus: Make voting easier and expand participation: universal mail ballots, fewer ID requirements, public campaign financing
dimensions.plus: Tighten election rules: stricter voter ID and verification, fewer mail-ballot accommodations

items.text: California should raise taxes on high earners and corporations to pay for more public services, like housing, transit, and health care.
California taxes are already too high. Government should live within its current budget, even if that means cutting some programs.
Apartment buildings should be allowed in neighborhoods that are currently zoned only for single-family homes.
Neighborhoods should have the final say over large new developments built near them.
Limits on how much landlords can raise rent each year should be expanded to more buildings.

items.text: People experiencing homelessness should be offered permanent housing first, without having to complete treatment beforehand.
Cities should clear encampments from sidewalks and parks, even when there aren't enough shelter beds for everyone.

items.text: California should phase out oil and gas drilling, even if it raises energy costs in the short term.
Environmental rules in California have gone too far and make gas, electricity, and housing too expensive.
The minimum wage should keep rising faster than inflation.
California should slow minimum-wage increases and new employer mandates to help small businesses survive.
Local police and jails should not help federal agents enforce immigration law.
State and local governments should cooperate fully with federal immigration enforcement.
Parents should be able to use public education funds at the school of their choice, including charter or private schools.
The growth of charter schools hurts traditional public schools and should be limited.

items.text: Access to abortion should be protected by law.
Schools should tell parents if their child asks to use a different name or pronouns at school, even if the child objects.
Gun laws should be stricter than they are now.
Law-abiding adults should be able to carry a concealed firearm without extensive restrictions.

Private insurance and market competition are the best ways to keep health care affordable.
Cities should convert some car lanes and parking into bus lanes and protected bike lanes.
Road improvements for drivers should be a higher priority than new transit projects.
Voters should have to show a government-issued photo ID to vote, including by mail.

contests.title: Measure A: Los Angeles County Charter Amendment Reiterating Good Faith Negotiation Obligations and Establishing Impartial Binding Arbitration for Certified Public Safety Employee Disputes
contests.summary: Amends the Los Angeles County Charter to prohibit strikes by district attorney investigators, medical examiners, and lifeguards, their supervisors, and nonadministrative civilian employees in the Fire Department, Sheriff's Department, and Department of Medical Examiner; reiterates existing good faith negotiation obligations; and establishes an impartial binding arbitration process for labor disputes with certified public safety employee organizations, including firefighters and sheriffs. Passes with a majority vote.

options.name: Steve Gibson
options.ballotDesignation: Governing Board Member, Pasadena Area Community College District

evidence.text: Gibson (board president, elected 2022) said: "My goal is to make sure PCC works for everyone: the recent graduate, the working parent, the neighbor retraining for a new career." Per his campaign, his record includes PCC Northwest at John Muir High School, expanded workforce training and accessibility.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Steve Gibson seeks second term on Pasadena City College board (July 2026)

evidence.text: Per his campaign, as a trustee Gibson supported fire-recovery training programs, including a new construction trades lab and expanded fire academy, electrical technology, welding and construction inspection programs.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Steve Gibson seeks second term on Pasadena City College board (July 2026)

evidence.text: Endorsed by the PCC Faculty Association, per his campaign announcement.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Steve Gibson seeks second term on Pasadena City College board (July 2026)

evidence.text: (2024) Gibson wrote that a trustee's role is to "ask tough questions and ensure accountability to our communities, especially our communities of color," and that graduation rates for Latino and Black students remain stagnant.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion: Steve Gibson, Why I support James Aragon for PCC Trustee (Mar 2024)

evidence.text: Campaign site: on the board, Gibson "introduced and championed a policy to decarbonize Pasadena City College."
evidence.title: Steve Gibson for Pasadena City College (campaign site)

evidence.text: In an Aug. 2025 column after losing his Altadena home in the Eaton Fire, Gibson urged the EPA to "uphold the Endangerment Finding" and called proposed climate rollbacks "a catastrophic step backward."
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion: PCC Trustee Steve Gibson, From Altadena to Washington: When Climate Change Hits Home, We Must Act (Aug. 2025)

evidence.text: (2022) Wrote that PCC part-time faculty "deserve more respect and equity," backing their calls for health insurance, job security and equal pay for equal work.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion: Dr. Steve Gibson, We Must Support Part-Time Faculty at PCC (2022)

evidence.text: Endorsed by the LA County Federation of Labor, Los Angeles County Democratic Party and Los Angeles League of Conservation Voters.
evidence.title: Steve Gibson for Pasadena City College (campaign site)

evidence.text: (2020) Opposed PUSD's $500 million Measure O facilities bond, citing failed oversight of the earlier Measure TT bond and calling Measure O "a blank check for a School District in need of reform."
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion | David Coher: No Oversight Means No on O (Oct. 2020)

evidence.text: (2020) As a Pasadena planning commissioner, wrote that "The Pasadena Way requires us to establish a civilian oversight commission for our Police Department."
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion | David Coher: Civilian Oversight is the Pasadena Way (June 2020)

evidence.text: (2023) Urged the City Council to keep Pasadena Water and Power's reference resource plan and reject eliminating greenhouse emissions by 2030, calling it infeasible and saying it would cost at least $1.35 billion more.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion | David B. Coher: Climate Change Requires Climate Responsibility (2023)

options.name: Kimberly Kenne
options.ballotDesignation: Board of Education Member, Pasadena Unified School District

evidence.text: In a June 2026 guest column, Kenne wrote that it is hard to tell how the district's $300+ million general fund is used and urged a revised 3-year LCAP that "can clearly show our community what actions are being planned to help our students and how those actions are being funded."
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion: Kimberly Kenne, Pasadena Unified Needs Spending Plans That the Public Can Understand and Believe (June 2026)

evidence.text: Kenne wrote that LCAP expenditures not matching the budget "has happened for several years in Pasadena Unified" and is "misleading the public," and that the plan should let the community hold the district "accountable for increasing student achievement."
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: Guest Opinion: Kimberly Kenne, Pasadena Unified Needs Spending Plans That the Public Can Understand and Believe (June 2026)

evidence.text: In May 2026 Kenne seconded Richardson Bailey's motion rejecting the consultant's school-consolidation equity analysis, which passed; Kenne said the board was "stopping the AB 1912 process."
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: PUSD Board Halts School Closure Plan, Two Trustees Served With Recall Notices (May 2026)

evidence.text: In Sept. 2026 Kenne was in the 4-3 majority that rejected tabling, then approved, a webpage posting data on possible school consolidations.
evidence.title: Colorado Boulevard: Pasadena Unified Board hears debate over school closures, campus maintenance and data webpage (Sept. 2026)

evidence.text: (2019) Per Patch, citing the Star-News, Kenne voted against closing three elementary schools, backing a failed option that would also have closed Don Benito; she warned, "We will probably be back here in two to three years, closing elementary schools again."
evidence.title: Patch: Pasadena Unified to close 3 schools despite objections (Sept. 2019)

evidence.text: Campaign site: says she worked to keep funding in the classroom, is "a strong supporter of neighborhood schools," and pushed for transparency on district finances "with a focus on legal and consultancy expenditures."
evidence.title: Kim Kenne for PUSD and Altadena (campaign site)

evidence.text: Endorsed by the Los Angeles County Democratic Party (District 1). Per the party's release, Kealing said the endorsement reflects her values of bringing people together, supporting families and strengthening public schools.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: LA County Democrats Endorse 4 Pasadena Unified Board Candidates

evidence.text: Per the party's release, her campaign focuses on building strong community schools, putting families at the center of decision-making, expanding student opportunities, and supporting educators and school employees.
evidence.title: Pasadena Now: LA County Democrats Endorse 4 Pasadena Unified Board Candidates

evidence.text: Per Colorado Boulevard, Kealing said losing her family's Altadena home in the Eaton Fire reinforced her belief in schools as community hubs; her campaign priorities include school-community partnerships and supporting educators and staff.
evidence.title: Colorado Boulevard: Felita Kealing announces bid for Pasadena Unified Board, District 1 (Aug. 2026)

evidence.text: Re-election platform: elevate student voices, strengthen accountability, prioritize classrooms, support educators and staff, expand career opportunities, and align district spending with student and family needs.

contests.title: Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
contests.summary: Changes the recall process for statewide officers: if the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected; for other recalled officers, the office remains vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law.

contests.title: Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes. Initiative Statute.
contests.summary: Authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of the purchase price of a qualified new home. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down; bonds are repaid from homeowners' mortgage payments, not by the State.

contests.title: Proposition 38: Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research. Initiative Statute.
contests.summary: Authorizes $8.4 billion in state general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, with half dedicated to cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer's disease. Funds are split between a single UC-affiliated nonprofit research institute and research grants for public or nonprofit institutions; recipients must sell resulting technology and drugs in California at 20% below the national average price.

contests.title: Proposition 39: Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
contests.summary: Prohibits voting by mail unless the voter designates a government-issued identification number in their registration, invalidates mail ballots lacking the last four digits of a matching ID number, and prohibits voting in person without presenting government-issued identification. Requires elections officials to annually report the share of voters whose citizenship status they have verified.

contests.title: Proposition 40: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
contests.summary: Imposes a one-time tax of up to 5% on certain taxpayers with covered assets valued over $1 billion (businesses, securities, art, collectibles, intellectual property; excluding real property and some pensions and retirement accounts). Allocates 90% of revenues to health care and 10% to food assistance or education-related programs.

contests.title: Proposition 41: Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
contests.summary: Prohibits any new state taxes that exclude their revenues from the state spending limit approved by voters in 1979. For statewide special taxes, requires a pre-election audit of programs that would receive funding and recurring audits of programs funded by special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026. States that conflicting measures on the same ballot are void if this measure receives more affirmative votes.

contests.title: Proposition 42: Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
contests.summary: Prohibits new state taxes on personal property, including business interests, intellectual property, and financial assets (including assets in retirement and investment accounts), and prohibits new state taxes that apply retroactively based on conduct or status before the tax's effective date. Applies to taxes enacted or taking effect on or after January 1, 2026; states that conflicting measures on the same ballot are void if this measure receives more affirmative votes.

contests.title: Proposition 43: Limits Voters' Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
contests.summary: Raises the vote needed to approve voter-initiated local special taxes (taxes dedicated to a specific purpose, placed on the ballot by signature gathering) from a majority to two-thirds, matching the requirement for special taxes placed on the ballot by local governments. Applies to voter-proposed measures approved after January 1, 2027.

contests.title: Proposition 44: Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% Of Revenue on Program Services. Initiative Statute.
contests.summary: Imposes penalties on nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers that spend less than 90% of revenue on 'program services' advancing their charitable purpose, with the Department of Public Health able to waive requirements in exceptional circumstances. Authorizes the Attorney General to publish guidance defining qualifying expenditures and authorizes criminal charges for false reports or artificially increasing the spending ratio.

contests.title: Proposition 45: Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.
contests.summary: Amends the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) to expedite environmental review for specified project categories (including most housing, transportation, water, health, wildfire mitigation, educational facility, internet access, and clean energy projects). Sets deadlines for public agencies to complete review and limits agencies' current obligation to consider project alternatives.
